column9: Match each organelle to its job in the cell.
column14: Nucleus :: Control center that holds the cell's DNA
column15: Ribosome :: Assembles proteins (protein synthesis)
column16: Mitochondrion :: Converts energy from food into usable ATP
column17: Lysosome :: Clean-up crew filled with enzymes that break down old parts
column18: Chloroplast :: Uses sunlight to make sugar (photosynthesis)
column19: Golgi apparatus :: Modifies, sorts, and packages proteins
column28: Nucleus = control center with DNA. Ribosome = protein synthesis. Mitochondrion = ATP (cellular respiration). Lysosome = clean-up crew with enzymes. Chloroplast = photosynthesis. Golgi = modifies, sorts, and packages proteins.
column29: Start with the nicknames: control center, powerhouse, clean-up crew.

column9: Which organelle is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
column14: Chloroplast
column15: Mitochondrion
column16: Ribosome
column17: Nucleus
column28: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, and animal cells don't have them. Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria, ribosomes, and a nucleus.
column29: Animals eat their food. Which organelle lets plants make their own?

column9: Animal cells are surrounded by a rigid cell wall.
column28: False. Animal cells have no cell wall; their only boundary is a flexible cell membrane.
column29: Think of a cheek cell. Is its edge stiff or flexible?

column9: The fluid part of the cytoplasm, which is 70 to 90% water, is called the ___.
column28: The cytosol is the watery fluid part of the cytoplasm (70 to 90% water). The cytoplasm is the whole gel-like material inside the membrane, including the cytosol, that holds the organelles.
column29: It is not the whole cytoplasm, just its liquid part. The name is a shorter cyto- word.

column9: The plant cell wall is made mostly of ___.
column14: phospholipids, a type of lipid
column15: cellulose, a polysaccharide
column16: proteins, made of amino acids
column17: nucleic acids such as DNA
column28: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, a polysaccharide (a carbohydrate built from long chains of sugar). Its tough fibers are what make celery stringy and wood strong. Plant cells also contain lipids, proteins, and DNA, but those are not what the wall is built from.
column29: It is the same material that makes celery stringy and wood strong.

column9: What are the jobs of the **smooth** endoplasmic reticulum?
column14: Storing DNA and controlling the cell's activities
column15: Making lipids and breaking down drugs and poisons
column16: Capturing sunlight and making sugar
column17: Packaging finished proteins to be shipped out of the cell
column28: The smooth ER makes lipids (phospholipids and steroids) and detoxifies drugs and poisons, which is why liver cells have so much of it. Storing DNA and controlling the cell are the nucleus's jobs, chloroplasts make sugar, and the Golgi packages proteins.
column29: Liver cells are packed with smooth ER. What does your liver do for your body?

column9: Plant cells, animal cells, and bacteria all have ribosomes.
column28: True. Plant cells, animal cells, and bacteria all have ribosomes, because all of them need to make proteins.
column29: Do all three kinds of cells need to make proteins? What builds proteins?

column9: Which structures are long, whip-like tails that help some cells move?
column14: Cilia
column15: Lysosomes
column16: Flagella
column17: Vacuoles
column28: Flagella are long, whip-like tails that move a cell. Cilia also help with movement, but they are many short hairs, not long tails. Lysosomes and vacuoles are sacs inside the cell, so neither one is a tail.
column29: Compare the two movement structures by number and length.

column9: The nucleolus, found in the center of the nucleus, makes ___.
column20: ribosomes|ribosome|the ribosomes|rRNA|ribosomal RNA|ribosomal subunits|ribosome subunits|ribosomal subunit
column28: The nucleolus is the dark center of the nucleus, and it makes ribosomes. The ribosomes then leave the nucleus to build proteins.
column29: It makes the tiny structures that build proteins.

column9: What is the main job of a vacuole?
column14: Storing water, salts, proteins, and carbohydrates
column15: Making proteins by following DNA's instructions
column16: Controlling all of the cell's activities
column17: Breaking down worn-out organelles and waste
column28: Vacuoles are storage sacs for water, salts, proteins, and carbohydrates. Ribosomes make proteins, the nucleus controls the cell, and lysosomes break down old parts.
column29: Picture the big water-filled sac in the middle of a plant cell. What is it doing?

column9: Which structure regulates what enters and leaves the cell?
column14: The nucleus
column15: The gel-like cytoplasm
column16: The cell membrane
column17: The nucleolus
column28: The cell membrane controls what goes in and out, and it also protects and supports the cell. The nucleus controls cell activities, but not traffic in and out.
column29: It is the boundary around every cell.

column9: The word **organelle** means ___.
column14: "organ system," a group of organs that work together
column15: "little organ," a specialized structure inside a cell
column16: "whole organism," a complete living thing
column17: "organ cell," one of the cells that make up an organ
column28: Organelles are "little organs": highly specialized structures inside eukaryotic cells, each with its own job, just like organs in your body. An organ system, a whole organism, and the cells of an organ are all much bigger than one organelle.
column29: A kitchenette is a small kitchen. What might the ending -elle add to the word organ?

column9: Microtubules and microfilaments are protein filaments that together make up the ___.
column28: The cytoskeleton is the cell's internal frame, made of microtubules and microfilaments. It maintains cell shape, moves things around, and is important in cell division.
column29: It is the cell's internal support network that keeps the cell's shape.

column9: The cells lining your windpipe sweep mucus and trapped dust up and away from your lungs. What do these cells use to do this?
column14: Cilia
column15: A flagellum
column16: A cell wall
column17: Lysosomes
column28: Windpipe cells are covered with cilia, many short hairs that beat together to sweep mucus and dust along, away from the lungs. A flagellum is a single tail, not a carpet of hairs. Windpipe cells are animal cells, so they have no cell wall, and lysosomes break down old parts instead of moving things.
column29: Each windpipe cell has many of these, not just one.

column9: Plants are not the only living things with cell walls; fungi, algae, and bacteria have them too.
column28: True. Plants, algae, fungi, and bacteria all have cell walls, so a cell wall by itself does not prove that a cell came from a plant.
column29: Think about mushrooms and pond scum. Do their cells have a stiff outer layer?

column9: What is the difference between rough ER and smooth ER?
column14: Rough ER has ribosomes attached to it; smooth ER does not.
column15: Smooth ER has ribosomes attached to it; rough ER does not.
column16: Rough ER is found only in plants; smooth ER only in animals.
column17: Rough ER stores DNA; smooth ER makes ATP.
column28: The ribosomes stuck to the rough ER make it look bumpy, and they build proteins there. Smooth ER has no ribosomes and makes lipids instead. Both are found in plant and animal cells.
column29: What makes the rough ER look "rough"?

column9: Which structures do plant cells have that animal cells do NOT? Select all that apply.
column14: Cell wall
column15: One large central vacuole
column16: Nucleus
column17: Mitochondria
column28: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole. Animal cells lack all three. Mitochondria, a nucleus, and ribosomes are in both.
column29: Remember the three plant-only features from the plant vs. animal chart.

column9: Put the steps in order to show how a cell makes a protein and sends it out of the cell.
column14: A ribosome assembles the protein
column15: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages the protein
column16: The protein leaves through the cell membrane
column17: The nucleus sends out the DNA's instructions
column18: The rough ER moves the protein along
column28: Nucleus (instructions) → ribosome (assembles the protein) → rough ER (moves it) → Golgi apparatus (modifies and packages it) → cell membrane (out of the cell). Proteins from the rough ER move to the Golgi.
column29: Start where the instructions are kept and end at the cell's outer boundary. What happens in between?

column9: Mr. Erickson's cell analogy project compares a cell to a factory. Match each organelle to its part of the factory.
column14: Nucleus :: Manager's office that holds the blueprints
column15: Ribosomes :: Workers who assemble the products
column16: Rough ER :: Assembly line where products are built and moved along
column17: Golgi apparatus :: Shipping department that packages and labels products
column18: Lysosomes :: Clean-up crew that breaks down trash
column19: Mitochondria :: Power plant that supplies energy
column28: Nucleus = manager's office with blueprints (DNA). Ribosomes = workers building proteins. Rough ER = assembly line. Golgi = shipping department that packages and labels. Lysosomes = clean-up crew. Mitochondria = power plant (ATP).
column29: Match the job, not the name: who gives orders, who builds, who packages, who cleans, who supplies power?

column9: In one student's Krusty Krab cell analogy, the restaurant building, with its OPEN/CLOSED sign, protects everyone inside and decides who can come in. Which cell structure does it stand for?
column14: The nucleus
column15: The mitochondria
column16: The Golgi apparatus
column17: The cell membrane
column28: The building surrounds and protects the restaurant and controls who enters, just as the cell membrane regulates what enters and leaves the cell. The nucleus gives orders, mitochondria supply energy, and the Golgi packages.
column29: Which structure is the boundary that controls what gets in and out?

column9: In her edible cell model, Hailey fills a bowl with lemon Jell-O that holds all the candy organelles in place. What does the Jell-O represent?
column14: The cell wall
column15: The nucleus
column16: The vacuole
column17: The cytoplasm
column28: The Jell-O is the gel-like material that fills the cell and holds the organelles, which is the cytoplasm. The bowl would be the boundary, and the nucleus and vacuole are organelles floating in the gel.
column29: What fills the space between the organelles?

column9: In a city analogy, which organelle is best compared to the city's warehouses and water towers?
column14: Vacuoles
column15: Ribosomes
column16: Lysosomes
column17: Chloroplasts
column28: Warehouses and water towers store supplies and water, just as vacuoles store water, salts, proteins, and carbohydrates. Ribosomes build, lysosomes break down, and chloroplasts make sugar.
column29: Warehouses and water towers store things. Which organelle stores materials?

column9: In a school analogy, which organelle is best compared to the custodians, who clean up trash and recycle broken things?
column14: Ribosomes
column15: Golgi apparatus
column16: Lysosomes
column17: Cell membrane
column28: Lysosomes are filled with enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and waste so the parts can be reused, like custodians cleaning and recycling. Ribosomes build proteins, the Golgi packages them, and the membrane controls entry.
column29: Which organelle is called the cell's clean-up crew?

column9: The cytoplasm is an organelle.
column28: False. The cytoplasm is the gel-like material that fills the cell and holds the organelles, but it is not an organelle itself. That is why the organelle chart lists it as "Cytoplasm (not an organelle)."
column29: An organelle is a specialized structure. Is the gel that fills the cell a structure?

column9: What is the cell membrane made of?
column14: Two layers of phospholipids (a phospholipid bilayer)
column15: A single layer of cellulose, like a plant cell wall
column16: A rigid wall of protein filaments called microtubules
column17: A double layer of DNA wrapped around the cell
column28: The cell membrane is a double lipid layer, the phospholipid bilayer, with proteins embedded in it. Cellulose is in the plant cell wall, protein filaments make the cytoskeleton, and DNA is in the nucleus.
column29: "Bi" means two. Which molecule from the macromolecules unit has a head and two tails?

column9: How are vacuoles in animal cells different from vacuoles in plant cells?
column14: Animal cells have no vacuoles at all; plant cells have one large one.
column15: Animal cells have just one small vacuole; plant cells have one large one.
column16: Animal cells have many small vacuoles; plant cells have one large one.
column17: There is no difference; both cells have one large central vacuole.
column28: Animal cells have many small vacuoles for storage. A plant cell has one large central vacuole that holds water and pushes out against the cell wall for support. Animal cells do store materials, so they are not missing vacuoles; they just have lots of small ones instead of one big one.
column29: Animal cells still need to store water, salts, and food. Without one big central sac, where could they keep it all?

column9: In the cell observation lab, Brody notices that his onion skin cells have no chloroplasts, but the winter wheat leaf cells are full of them. What is the best explanation?
column14: Onion cells get their sugar from the soil, so they never need chloroplasts.
column15: The onion cells lost their chloroplasts when the slide was stained.
column16: The onion's cell wall blocks the view, so its chloroplasts can't be seen.
column17: The bulb's inner layers are kept from light, so they don't do photosynthesis.
column28: A cell's organelles match its job. Onion skin comes from the bulb's fleshy inner layers, which are leaves wrapped inside the bulb and shut off from light, so they have no use for chloroplasts. Leaf cells sit in the sunlight and are packed with them. Plants don't absorb sugar from the soil, staining doesn't remove chloroplasts, and the wheat cells have walls too, yet their chloroplasts show up clearly.
column29: Is the inside of an onion bulb ever in sunlight? Does a cell make parts it has no use for?

column9: Mia stains potato cells with iodine and sees many black dots in each cell. Iodine turns black when it touches starch. What does this tell you about the job of potato cells?
column14: They make proteins for the whole plant.
column15: They capture sunlight to make sugar by photosynthesis.
column16: They store food for the plant to use later.
column17: They protect the plant from bacteria.
column28: Iodine shows starch, so the black dots are stored starch, which is food. A potato is an underground storage organ: its cells take in sugar sent down from the leaves and build it into starch, which the plant uses to sprout and grow next spring. The potato cells store food; they don't make sugar by photosynthesis, since they grow underground in the dark. Iodine tests for starch, not for proteins or protection against bacteria.
column29: Think about what a potato is for. What does it do next spring when it sprouts?

column9: Under the microscope at 400x, each Elodea leaf cell is packed with dozens of small green ovals. These green ovals are ___.
column28: The small green ovals are chloroplasts. They contain the green pigment that captures light energy for photosynthesis, which is why plant leaf cells are full of them.
column29: Which organelle carries out photosynthesis?

column9: Muscle cells use a lot of energy to contract. Which organelle would you expect to find in especially large numbers in muscle cells?
column14: Chloroplasts
column15: Vacuoles
column16: Cell walls
column17: Mitochondria
column28: Mitochondria convert energy from food into ATP (cellular respiration happens here), so cells that use lots of energy, like muscle cells, have lots of them. Muscle cells are animal cells, so they have no chloroplasts or cell walls.
column29: Which organelle makes the ATP that muscles use?

column9: Which structures help a cell move or move materials around? Select all that apply.
column14: Vacuoles
column15: Lysosomes
column16: Flagella
column17: Cytoskeleton
column28: Cilia (short hairs) and flagella (long whips) move the cell, and the cytoskeleton's protein filaments move materials inside the cell. Lysosomes digest, vacuoles store, and the nucleolus makes ribosomes.
column29: Think about what a cell uses to move itself, and what carries things around inside it.

column9: What does the nuclear envelope (nuclear membrane) do?
column14: Makes proteins in the dark center of the nucleus
column15: Converts sugar into ATP to power the nucleus
column16: Surrounds the nucleus and keeps the DNA separate
column17: Holds all of the cell's organelles in a gel-like fluid
column28: The nuclear envelope is the membrane around the nucleus that keeps the DNA separate from the cytoplasm. The nucleolus makes ribosomes, mitochondria make ATP, and the cytoplasm is the gel.
column29: "Envelope" is a clue: what does an envelope do to a letter?

column9: Jada is building a 3D cell model. Which organelle should she show as a stack of flattened sacs (like a stack of pancakes) near the ER?
column14: Mitochondrion
column15: Lysosome
column16: Nucleus
column17: Golgi apparatus
column28: The Golgi apparatus looks like a stack of flattened sacs. Proteins from the rough ER move into it to be modified, sorted, and packaged. Mitochondria are bean-shaped, lysosomes are small round sacs, and the nucleus is a large sphere.
column29: Which organelle receives proteins from the rough ER?

column9: Which organelle should a cell model show as a bean shape with a folded inner membrane?
column14: Ribosome
column15: Chloroplast
column16: Mitochondrion
column17: Vacuole
column28: Mitochondria are bean-shaped with a highly folded inner membrane, which gives more space for the reactions that make ATP. Ribosomes are tiny dots, chloroplasts are green ovals with stacks inside, and vacuoles are sacs.
column29: The folds give extra surface area for the reactions that release energy from food.

column9: Which material would best represent the cell membrane of an animal cell in a 3D model?
column14: A cardboard shoe box
column15: A brick
column16: A plastic sandwich bag
column17: A wooden picture frame
column28: The cell membrane is flexible, so a plastic bag is a good match. A cardboard box, a brick, or a wooden frame is rigid, which would better represent a plant cell wall, and animal cells have no wall.
column29: Is the animal cell's boundary stiff or flexible?

column9: A cell's lysosomes stop working. What would most likely happen?
column14: The cell would stop making ATP for energy.
column15: The cell could no longer assemble any of its proteins.
column16: The cell would lose the DNA in its nucleus.
column17: Old organelles and waste would build up in the cell.
column28: Lysosomes are the clean-up crew: their enzymes break down old organelles, lipids, carbohydrates, and proteins. Without them, waste piles up. ATP comes from mitochondria, proteins from ribosomes, and DNA is in the nucleus.
column29: What does the clean-up crew do? What happens when nobody takes out the trash?

column9: Three students built plant cell models. Ana's has a cell wall with a cell membrane just inside it, chloroplasts, mitochondria, a nucleus, and a large central vacuole. Ben's has chloroplasts and a nucleus but no cell wall, "because the membrane is enough." Cal's has a cell membrane, mitochondria, and a nucleus, but no cell wall and no chloroplasts. Which model is most accurate for a plant cell?
column14: Ben's model
column15: Cal's model
column16: Ben's and Cal's models are equally accurate
column17: Ana's model
column28: Ana included all three plant-only features: cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole. She also kept the cell membrane just inside the wall and the mitochondria that plant cells have too. Ben left out the cell wall, which plant cells have outside the membrane. Cal's model is really an animal cell: no wall and no chloroplasts.
column29: Check each model for the three plant-only features.

column9: Ethan writes, "The cell wall controls what enters and leaves a plant cell." What is the best evaluation?
column14: Correct: the cell wall is the only outer boundary that a plant cell has.
column15: Incorrect: the membrane controls what enters; the wall gives support.
column16: Correct: the cell membrane is found only in animal cells.
column17: Incorrect: the nucleus controls what enters and leaves.
column28: The rigid cellulose wall supports and protects the cell. Inside it, the cell membrane regulates what goes in and out. Plant cells have both, and the nucleus controls cell activities, not traffic through the boundary.
column29: Plant cells have two boundaries. Which one is selective?

column9: A cell's Golgi apparatus stops working. What would happen to the proteins made on the rough ER?
column14: They would never be assembled in the first place.
column15: They would not get modified, sorted, and packaged.
column16: They would be broken down into ATP right away.
column17: They would be turned into DNA in the nucleus.
column28: Ribosomes and the rough ER can still make proteins, but the next step, modifying, sorting, and packaging in the Golgi, would stop. The proteins would not get finished and sent where they belong.
column29: In the protein pathway, what step comes right after the rough ER?

column9: A poison blocks the mitochondria in a cell. What would most likely happen?
column14: The cell couldn't make enough ATP, so jobs that need energy would slow or stop.
column15: The cell would stop making sugar, because mitochondria make the cell's glucose.
column16: Old parts and waste would pile up, because mitochondria are the clean-up crew.
column17: The cell would stop making proteins, because mitochondria assemble them.
column28: Mitochondria convert energy from food into ATP. Without ATP, jobs that need energy (building proteins, moving, active transport) slow down or stop. Protein building may slow too, but only because it runs short of ATP; ribosomes, not mitochondria, assemble proteins. Mitochondria break sugar down instead of making it (chloroplasts make sugar), and lysosomes, not mitochondria, are the clean-up crew.
column29: What does the cell's powerhouse make?

column9: A plant cell already has chloroplasts to capture energy from sunlight. Why does it also need mitochondria?
column14: Chloroplasts make sugar; mitochondria turn that sugar into usable ATP.
column15: It doesn't need them; plant cells have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria.
column16: Mitochondria make sugar at night when the chloroplasts are off.
column17: Mitochondria store the extra water made by photosynthesis.
column28: Chloroplasts store the sun's energy in sugar, but the cell can't use sugar directly. Mitochondria break the sugar down in cellular respiration to make ATP, day and night. Plant cells do have mitochondria, and mitochondria don't make sugar or store water.
column29: What does each organelle actually produce, and which product can the cell spend on its jobs?

column9: Dominic's cell model shows ribosomes only inside the Golgi apparatus, and his rough ER has nothing on it. What is the best correction?
column14: Remove the ribosomes, because animal cells don't have any.
column15: Put ribosomes free in the cytoplasm and dotted along the rough ER.
column16: Move all of the ribosomes inside the nucleus with the DNA.
column17: Leave it as it is; ribosomes really do belong inside the Golgi apparatus.
column28: Ribosomes are free floating in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough ER, which is what makes it rough. The Golgi receives new proteins from the rough ER to modify and package; it doesn't hold the ribosomes. Animal and plant cells both have ribosomes.
column29: What makes rough ER look rough?

column9: Which of these are membrane-bound organelles, each wrapped in its own membrane? Select all that apply.
column14: Mitochondrion
column15: Chloroplast
column16: Cytoplasm
column17: Lysosome
column28: Mitochondria, chloroplasts, lysosomes, and the Golgi apparatus are each wrapped in their own membrane; these membrane-bound organelles are found only in eukaryotic cells. Ribosomes have no membrane; even bacteria, which have no membrane-bound organelles, have ribosomes. The cytoplasm is the gel that fills the cell, not an organelle.
column29: Which ones are also found in bacteria? Those can't be membrane-bound.

column9: Under the microscope, onion cells look like neat rectangular bricks, but cheek cells are rounded and uneven. Which structure best explains the difference?
column14: Cheek cells have many more chloroplasts than onion cells do.
column15: Onion cells have no cell membrane, only a wall.
column16: Cheek cells have a larger central vacuole inside.
column17: Onion cells have a rigid cell wall; cheek cells do not.
column28: The stiff cellulose wall holds plant cells in a boxy shape. Animal cells have only a flexible membrane, so their shape is rounder and can change. Cheek cells have no chloroplasts or large central vacuole, and onion cells do have a membrane inside the wall.
column29: Which plant-only structure is rigid?

column9: Every model has limits. Noah's animal cell model is a plastic bag of clear gelatin with candy organelles set in place, including a large gumball for the nucleus. Which is a real weakness of his model?
column14: Real cells are flat, like they look on a slide, so a 3D model is misleading.
column15: His nucleus is the biggest candy, but the nucleus is one of the smallest organelles.
column16: The bag is flexible, but an animal cell's boundary is really stiff and rigid.
column17: The candy organelles sit still, but real organelles move and are always working.
column28: Every model simplifies something. In a living cell, organelles are always working and get moved around (in the Elodea lab you can watch chloroplasts circle the edge of each cell), but candy set in gelatin just sits there. The other choices are not weaknesses: real cells are 3D and only look flat because a slide is so thin, the nucleus is usually the largest organelle, and an animal cell's membrane really is flexible.
column29: Check each choice against what you know about real cells. A weakness is something about real cells that the model gets wrong.

column9: A sperm cell has a long flagellum and is packed with mitochondria. What is the best explanation for this combination?
column14: The flagellum moves the cell, and the mitochondria store the food it needs for the trip.
column15: The flagellum moves the cell, and the mitochondria make the ATP it needs to swim.
column16: The mitochondria move the cell, and the flagellum makes the ATP it needs to swim.
column17: The flagellum moves the cell, and the mitochondria build the proteins it is made of.
column28: A sperm cell's job is to swim. The flagellum is the whip that moves it, and swimming takes lots of energy, so its many mitochondria make the ATP it needs. Mitochondria don't store food (vacuoles store materials), they don't build the flagellum's proteins (ribosomes assemble proteins), and they don't move the cell; the flagellum moves it but makes no ATP. A cell's parts match its job.
column29: What is a sperm cell's job, and what does that job need?

column9: A cell's DNA still holds the instructions for a protein, but all of the cell's ribosomes are damaged. What will happen?
column14: The protein cannot be assembled, even though the instructions exist.
column15: The nucleus will assemble the protein instead.
column16: The Golgi apparatus will build the whole protein from scratch instead.
column17: The protein will be made normally by the lysosomes.
column28: The nucleus holds the instructions, but ribosomes are the only structures that assemble proteins. With no working ribosomes, the instructions can't be followed. The Golgi only modifies and packages proteins that ribosomes have already assembled, and lysosomes break things down.
column29: Who reads the instructions and actually builds the protein?

column9: Pancreas cells make the protein insulin and release it into the blood. Which organelle is LEAST directly involved in making and releasing insulin?
column14: Nucleus
column15: Rough ER
column16: Smooth ER
column17: Golgi apparatus
column28: Insulin's instructions come from the nucleus, ribosomes on the rough ER assemble it, the rough ER moves it along, and the Golgi apparatus modifies and packages it before it leaves the cell. The smooth ER has no ribosomes; it makes lipids and detoxifies drugs and poisons, so it is the least involved in making and releasing a protein like insulin.
column29: Trace the protein pathway from the instructions to the cell membrane. Which of these is not on it?

column9: A drug destroys the cytoskeleton of an animal cell. Which problem would most likely result?
column14: It couldn't control what enters and leaves, because the cytoskeleton is its boundary.
column15: It would lose its shape and have trouble moving materials and dividing.
column16: It could no longer make ATP, because the cytoskeleton is what powers the cell.
column17: Nothing would change, because only plant cells need support from inside.
column28: The cytoskeleton's protein filaments support the cell, maintain its shape, move materials, and are important in cell division. Without it, an animal cell would lose its shape. The cell membrane, not the cytoskeleton, is the boundary that controls what enters and leaves, and mitochondria make ATP. Animal cells need their cytoskeleton for support even more than plant cells do, because they have no cell wall.
column29: What jobs does the cytoskeleton do in the notes? Picture an animal cell with no frame inside.

column9: Leo's city analogy: nucleus = city hall, mitochondria = power plant, cell membrane = city limits with checkpoints, chloroplasts = solar panel farm. He labels it "Animal Cell City." What is the problem?
column14: Animal cells have no nucleus, so there should be no city hall.
column15: Animal cells have no chloroplasts, so the solar farm doesn't fit.
column16: Mitochondria should be the city limits, not the power plant.
column17: Cell membranes are found only in plant cells, not animal cells.
column28: Every pairing works, but chloroplasts are never found in animal cells. Either remove the solar farm or rename it a plant cell city (and add a cell wall, like a city wall). Animal cells do have a nucleus and a membrane, and mitochondria fit the power plant.
column29: Which organelle in his list is never found in animal cells?
